Dear Raghav Bhaiya,
Don't tell Amma I'm telling you this first. I got selected for the national astronomy camp. Only twelve students from our state. When the list came out, Ma'am wanted to announce it in assembly, and I begged her not to.
In class, when someone asked, I laughed and said, 'They probably mixed up my roll number.' Everyone laughed too. It felt safer than saying I'm thrilled. Because I am. I've wanted this since I was nine.
But you remember what happened to Sreeja when she topped the boards? The whole group started calling her Madam Genius and stopped saving her a seat. I don't want to be Madam Genius.
Is it stupid to hide something this good?
Vidya

Because every time my older cousin Kunal won anything, the aunties at family dinners said he'd 'changed' and 'thinks he's too good for us.' I was scared that would be me. So I shrank it. Silly, right? Anyway, I lost in the quarterfinals. I didn't even tell you that.

Monday. The email came during break: Vaibhav had made it to the national quiz finals in Delhi, one of eight from the whole country. Indu read it over his shoulder and squealed. Vaibhav shut the laptop. "They needed someone from the east zone. Pure luck."
Thursday. Mr Fernandes announced it in class. Heads turned. Vaibhav slid down in his seat and said, loud enough, "Don't worry, I'll be out in round one." People laughed. At lunch he skipped the prep session in the library so nobody would see him studying.
The next Tuesday. Walking home, Indu stopped him. "You can actually be happy, you know. Nobody's going to hate you for it." Vaibhav kicked a stone. "They called Rishi 'Mr Topper' for a year." He paused. "I am happy. I'm scared to look it."

qa.a: Eight, and Vaibhav was one of them.

qa.a: He fears that looking proud will make friends turn cold, the way Rishi was called "Mr Topper" for a year.

qa.a: Indu tells him he can be happy and he admits being scared to look it; once said aloud, he might go back to the prep sessions openly.

qa.a: Indu seems to want to celebrate with him and may feel a bit sad, or even pushed away, when he keeps joking it off.

passage: Sit, Abhinav. You've been telling everyone your chess selection was "a mistake," so let your Irfan Chacha tell you something. In 1994 I was fifteen and I got picked for the national junior painting competition. The whole district, only me. Our headmaster wanted a photo in the paper. I begged him not to. In class I said, "They must have mixed up my painting with someone good." Everyone laughed, and I felt safe. When my friends asked about Mumbai, I said I'd probably just go to eat the food. I was afraid that if I looked proud, they'd call me big-headed and stop sitting with me. So I went, I painted, I came fourth, and I told nobody. I still have that certificate in a tin. Fourth in India, beta. I wish I had let myself enjoy it for one week.

qa.a: He was picked for the national junior painting competition.

qa.a: He worried his friends would call him big-headed and stop sitting with him.

qa.a: Abhinav could tell friends plainly about the selection and the excitement, instead of calling it a mistake, and enjoy it while it lasts.

qa.a: Most might be happy for him or curious about the tournament, and his jokes may be hiding a chance for them to cheer.
